posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
In order to fit in a brewsters window to the existing cavity it will need to be placed on one of two mostly identical locations.

![Image](http://www.designerinlight.com/ssy1oc.jpg)

Here is a picture of the end I am assuming is the Output side. It shows the mirror the metal basket that holds the mirror and two of the three feet that set the mirror alignment. The little hole right behind the red wire is about 6mm wide and 8mm deep. I have not taken off the mirror to measure.

The mirrors are flat so I expect this is a multi-mode beam. (I'll research this more. I just broke out my copy of "Solid State Laser Engineering".) Because the mounting system is so simple I would expect a set of mirrors could be installed to make this a TEM 00 laser. The mirrors are about 13mm dia and 5.5 mm thick. The cavity is 92 mm long.

One way that comes to mind would be to drill to 1/16" holes into the frame that holds the mirrors, place the brwester's window inside and drop glue into the holes. posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
> **Sergio:** Colin are the two mirrors internally (face to face) flat? In this case a very difficult way to build a stable laser, probably a high FL from one mirror is present?As Brewster windows, some Ar ion laser dead heads have mounted metal supports already with the right angle to be glued at the right end corner of this laser.

Yes, they are perfectly flat. You can easily see inside the cavity and make them reflect an image to prove they are flat.

This cavity is very small without much room. It is very clever of Bill to have figured out a way to make the brewster's fit at all.

I think an aperture placed inside might help the performance as well, but without a radiused mirror set and a longer cavity I suspect TEM00 operation is impossible. It would be fairly easy to make two of them have a longer cavity. Mirrors for this laser should be fairly easy to find but I have not searched yet. 

It is actually a pretty interesting starting place for a compact pulsed laser. I suspect within a month one of us will be able to make a perfect hologram of a rose or something of the like. Catching an insect would make a good subject.

Making one be an amplifier is a good idea as well. There are many options but one is to take the second one and remove the optics and the Q-switch and place it ahead of the frequency doubler. This may make the beam have a significant amount of divergence however. One would have to try it to know.

Another experiment worth trying is to remove the HR (Highly Reflective) mirror from one and the OC (Output Coupler) and Q-switch from the other and put them in-line. This would make the cavity longer and would give the energy of both flash lamps to the beam. Adding a 3 to 4mm aperture would help create a TEM00 profile. To alligh both cavities, take a visable laser with a small divergence and align it through the mirrors so that all the spots created align. (The mirrors are only slightly reflective to any frequency other than 1064nm so the spots are faint but visable.)

I have a little card that glows a spot when exposed to IR. It is useful to find out how the beam shape works out. I don't remember where I got it. I got it and some Safety Goggles when I was playing with green lasers. The safety goggles are pretty cool, they are coated to ND10 for 1064nm, 808nm and 532nm. Great if you are inside a C315 or the like.

A 532nm coated interference mirror from an old laser placed at 45 degrees to the beam at the output would make a good IR filter to take the IR out of the output.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Also, having the beam diverge before the frequency doubler will lower the conversion efficiency. Frequency doubling crystals are angle dependent and having parts of the beam at different angles is not ideal.

Does anyone know how to calculate the crystal thickness for optimum frequency doubling efficiency?

> **Bill Jensen:** Here is how to wire up the SSY-1, Pulse Forming Network, and the trigger boards that you get on Ebay for $150:Starting fromhttp://www.repairfaq.org/sam/pfn1sch.pdfWe run the + high voltage (700 nominal, 800 pushing it, 950 absolute max that capacitor can take) through a 3.9 K ohm 10 Watt resistor to P1-9. The negative goes to the black wire with the spade lug with circular hole in it, which is found next to the HV red output for the Flashlamp. All grounds go here.The P1-5 gets +26.5 volts 100 mA but it works even at 16 v. The ground is P1-15. Keep it powered up as long as the HV is applied. When the power is shut off, remove this voltage source to quickly drain the cap voltage in about 2 seconds, its a safely.P1-13 is ground and P1-3 is some sort of trigger voltage, but I was not able to figure it out.Plug the 4 pin green connector between the PFN board and the red trigger transformer board.The lamp positive is red FL+ and the neg of flamp is black to FL-. The white trigger wire of the lamp goes to the red wire from the trigger transformer. Insulate it for 30KV.I shorted the case of the scr to the larger of the 2 vertical terminals that poke up from the SCR. Very little current / power throught it, but hundreds of volts so insulate well.Insulate the Red trigger wire with thick insulation wire.The caps charge to 700 volts in under a second. It flashes with a short on SCR. Sometimes you may get a double pulse if the switch contacts bounce. The current through the 3.9Kohms is not enough to support flashlamp conduction and it extinguishes.

posts.author: Bill Jensen
posts.content_md:
Hi Colin,

Looks like you are having fun !

The SCR is the one on the red "firecracker" board, and has the Hexnut. Shorting the indicated places with a Normally Open switch will fire the trigger fine. Cap voltage is measured from the side of the resistor next to the cap. (The other side of the resistor goes to the + of the HV power supply.) The ground of the voltmeter goes to the black wire with the metal lug with round hole in it. 

That HV supply is nice to be a variable one. A variac with a transformer and bridge rectifier can be an inexpensive option. I bought parts for an inexpensive power supply for this laser SSY1 to make sure it works. If so, I can sell some that are tested, maybe for $100.

Sincerely,

Bill Jensen

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
> **Bill Jensen:** We run the + high voltage (700 nominal, 800 pushing it, 950 absolute max that capacitor can take) through a 3.9 K ohm 10 Watt resistor to P1-9.

In looking at the supplied connectors It would seem that the Large Red wire from the Cap would go straight to the flash lamp. What is the purpose of the 3.9 K resistor?

posts.author: Bill Jensen
posts.content_md:
Hi Colin,

The caps' red wire goes to the flashlamp. It also goes to the 3.9 K ohm resistor (10W) which then goes to the positive of the charging power supply. It serves to limit the current from the power supply to the cap.

Here is the sequence of discharge, after the cap is charged over about 1/2 a second, you are ready to discharge by triggering. Upon triggering the cap dumps all the charge in it through the smoothing and limiting inductor in the PFN. In the meantime the HV source tries to charge up the cap again, but can't overcome the massive drain from the flashlamp conducting. With the 3.9K the lamp then extinguishes and then the HV power supply can charge back up the cap. If you didn't have it, the power supply would deliver a lot of current (possibly burning it up) and keep the flashlamp glowing. Not what we want.

I hope that helps.

Sincerely,

Bill Jensen
